title: Arizona joins Nevada to fight proposed cuts to their shares of Colorado River

Photograph: George Frey/Getty Images Colorado river crisis Arizona joins Nevada to fight proposed cuts to their shares of Colorado River Move comes after Trump administration announced restrictions that could slash water supplies Uwa Ede-Osifo Sat 17 Oct 2026 19.40 EDT Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 20.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Arizona has joined Nevada in its legal battle against the Trump administration’s proposed cuts to their shares of the shrinking Colorado River. The move comes after the interior department announced restrictions this summer that could slash the water supplied to lower basin states – Arizona, California and Nevada – over the next two years depending on the river’s condition. The river’s major reservoirs, Lake Mead and Lake Powell, have plummeted to historically low levels, due to overuse and a changing climate. The states sharing the waterway were at an impasse with the upper basin states arguing that their downstream counterparts were responsible for the reservoir’s water shortages and should thus face the largest cuts. The federal government’s intervention came after the states missed several deadlines for a consensus. The fear looming over the state of the river is that if reservoir levels plunged far enough, the waterway would effectively not be able to flow downstream, a so-called deadpool. The upper basin states – Wyoming, Colorado, Utah and New Mexico – were spared from the water cuts, an exemption that has drawn sharp rebuke from the leaders of the lower basin states. “We are drawing a line in the sand,” Arizona governor Katie Hobbs said in a Friday statement . “I am taking this legal action alongside Nevada because the federal government refuses to hold the Upper Basin accountable for the water deliveries they owe Arizona , and is threatening to force draconian cuts that go well beyond the Lower Basin Agreement,” Hobbs continued, referring to a two-year-voluntary water conservation pact among her state, California and Nevada. Tom Buschatzke, the director of Arizona’s water department, said “intervention in the Nevada lawsuit is necessary at this time for Arizona to protect its legal rights to Colorado River water while preserving a path forward to achieving a collaborative outcome with California and Nevada to protect the Colorado River system”. An interior department spokesperson called Hobbs “wrong” in a statement and claimed that the department would operate in good faith. “It’s unfortunate to see Arizona playing politics instead of working toward meaningful solutions,” the statement said. “Litigation won’t create a single additional drop of water or change the hydrologic realities facing the Colorado River Basin.” Explore more on these topics Colorado river crisis Arizona Nevada Rivers US politics Trump administration Water news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Original reporting and incisive analysis, direct from the Guardian every morning Sign up for our email About us Help Complaints & corrections Contact us Tip us off SecureDrop Privacy policy Cookie policy Tax strategy Terms & conditions All topics All writers Newsletters Digital newspaper archive Bluesky Facebook Instagram LinkedIn Threads TikTok YouTube Advertise with us Guardian Labs Work with us Accessibility settings Back to top © 2026 Guardian News & Media Limited or its affiliated companies.
